title: Zeppole
subtitle: neapolitan fried dough balls dusted with icing sugar
excerpt: Zeppole are light, puffy Neapolitan pastries made from a choux-style dough that is fried until golden and hollow inside, then dusted generously with icing sugar. The dough comes together quickly in a single saucepan and the frying takes less than 20 minutes. Serves 4.
sourceNotes: Zeppole are traditional Neapolitan pastries eaten on the feast of Saint Joseph on 19 March, which is also Father's Day in Italy. They are found across southern Italy in many forms, some baked, some fried, some filled with pastry cream. This version is the simplest: plain fried dough dusted with icing sugar.

glossaryTerms.definition: Neapolitan fried dough balls made from choux pastry, traditionally eaten on St Joseph's Day.
A light cooked pastry dough made by beating eggs into a hot butter and flour mixture, used for profiteroles, eclairs and zeppole.

content.text: dough cooked in the saucepan first, then beaten with eggs until glossy and smooth. When this dough hits hot oil it puffs rapidly and turns golden, producing a light, hollow ball with a crisp outside and airy inside. This recipe serves 4 and makes around 20 small zeppole.

The oil temperature is the most important variable. Too cool and the zeppole will be dense and greasy. Too hot and the outside will brown before the inside is cooked through. Aim for 170C to 175C and fry in small batches to keep the temperature stable.
Put the water, butter and caster sugar in a medium saucepan over medium heat. Stir until the butter has melted and the mixture comes to the boil.

Remove the pan from the heat and tip in all the flour at once. Beat vigorously with a wooden spoon until the dough comes together and pulls cleanly away from the sides of the pan. Return to low heat and stir for 1 to 2 minutes to cook out the flour.

Tip the dough into a bowl and leave to cool for 5 minutes. Add the beaten eggs a little at a time, beating well after each addition. The dough is ready when it is smooth, shiny and drops reluctantly from the spoon in a thick ribbon. Season to taste.
Pour enough neutral oil into a large deep frying pan to reach 5cm in depth. Heat to 170C to 175C.

Drop heaped teaspoons of dough into the oil in batches of 4 or 5 at a time. Fry for 3 to 4 minutes, turning occasionally, until evenly golden all over. They will puff and roll in the oil as they cook. Drain on kitchen paper.
Dust generously with icing sugar and serve straight away while still warm.

attrs.symptom: Zeppole are dense and greasy rather than light
attrs.cause: Oil temperature was too low, so the dough absorbed fat rather than puffing quickly
attrs.fix: Use a thermometer and keep the oil between 170C and 175C; fry in small batches to avoid cooling the oil

attrs.symptom: Dough is dropping off the spoon too easily and spreading flat in the oil
attrs.cause: Too much egg was added or it was added before the dough had cooled enough
attrs.fix: Cool the dough for at least 5 minutes before adding eggs, and add them gradually, checking the consistency after each addition

attrs.symptom: Zeppole are browning on the outside but raw in the middle
attrs.fix: Reduce heat until the oil settles at 170C; a thermometer is the only reliable way to check this

content.text: Zeppole are made across southern Italy in many variations. In Naples they are sold from street stalls on 19 March, the feast of Saint Joseph, which doubles as Father's Day in Italy. Bakeries queue around the block. Some versions are baked rather than fried, and some are filled with pastry cream or jam. This plain fried version is the most ancient and the quickest to make at home.
